analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans new offshore oil and gas drilling off the Atlantic coast.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced in May 2011 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to permanently bar the Interior Department from issuing any lease for oil, gas, or mineral exploration, development, or production in the Mid-Atlantic and North Atlantic planning areas, stretching roughly from New England to the Carolinas. The goal is to keep drilling away from the Atlantic coast permanently, rather than leaving the decision to each administration. It was introduced by Senator Menendez with three fellow Democrats from Atlantic coast states and never moved in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Atlantic coastal communities whose economies run on tourism, beach recreation, and commercial and recreational fishing, since a single spill could close beaches and damage fisheries for years; it also protects them from the industrial traffic and infrastructure that offshore drilling brings near shore.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Atlantic coastal tourism and fishing communities

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a permanent prohibition to the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act barring the Interior Secretary from issuing any lease for exploration, development, or production of oil, natural gas, or other minerals in the Mid-Atlantic and North Atlantic planning areas.

Because the ban is written into statute rather than left to administration-by-administration leasing plans, drilling off the Atlantic coast could not be restarted by a future Interior Department without another act of Congress.

The prohibition covers both the North Atlantic and Mid-Atlantic planning areas, the federal waters closest to New England, the Mid-Atlantic, and Chesapeake Bay-region coastlines where tourism and fishing are major employers.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies lose the chance to bid on Atlantic leases, and the federal government forgoes whatever royalties and revenue future Atlantic production might have generated.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies; potential federal royalties

drawbacks.text: A permanent statutory ban forgoes any domestic energy production and royalty revenue from the Mid-Atlantic and North Atlantic planning areas, closing them off by law even if future technology made drilling there safer or more economically attractive.

The ban is absolute: unlike a leasing plan, which an administration can revise every five years based on current conditions, the bill gives Congress no regular review of whether the prohibition still makes sense.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Atlantic coast states, the protection is concrete and permanent: their tourism and fishing economies are highly exposed to spill damage, and federal waters there had no significant production history to offset. The cost is forgone energy production and royalties in an area that was not producing oil anyway, plus the loss of flexibility to revisit the question as conditions change. On balance the bill's benefit is real but regional, and its cost is speculative.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Menendez introduced the bill on May 9, 2011, with Senators Lautenberg, Mikulski, and Cardin as cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources that same day.
No hearing, markup, vote, or floor action ever followed; the complete action history consists of introduction and committee referral.
No permanent Atlantic drilling ban became law during the 112th Congress, leaving the question of Atlantic leasing to future administrations' leasing plans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No permanent protection was enacted, and the offshore oil industry faced no new legal barrier to Atlantic drilling; future administrations retained full discretion over whether to open the area.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The offshore oil industry and any administration wanting Atlantic leases

for.name: Robert Menendez
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey (bill sponsor)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the COAST Anti-Drilling Act to permanently ban Atlantic offshore drilling.

for.name: Frank Lautenberg
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey (original cosponsor)

against.name: Jeff Bingaman
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or committee vote on the bill after it was referred to the committee.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's sponsor and cosponsors were all Democrats, and the Democratic chair of the Energy Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would permanently close the Mid-Atlantic and North Atlantic planning areas to oil and gas leasing, eliminating any future access to those federal waters. Its potential gain from drilling there carries the spill and industrial risk that coastal communities would bear.

industries.industry: Atlantic coastal tourism and commercial fishing
industries.note: These industries depend on clean beaches and healthy fisheries and would benefit from a statutory guarantee that drilling cannot be opened nearby. They get the protection without bearing any cost.
